title: Humanity’s deepest hole got only a third of the way through the crust
body: On 24 May 1970 Soviet scientists began drilling on the Kola Peninsula, aiming for 15,000 metres. By 1989 the Kola Superdeep Borehole reached **12,262 metres**, still the deepest anyone has drilled vertically into the Earth, yet only about a third of the way through the 35 km-thick continental crust beneath it. The rock turned out hotter than expected, about 180 °C at the bottom, which halted the deepest hole in 1992; the project ended in 1995 for lack of money. Along the way the drill found water pooled 3 to 6 km down, microscopic plankton fossils at 6 km, and none of the basalt layer expected at 7 km.

slides.alt: A to-scale column of the 35-kilometre-thick crust with the Kola borehole drawn as a thin line reaching 12,262 metres, about a third of the way down, with depth marks at 10, 20 and 30 kilometres.
slides.caption: The crust under Kola is about 35 km thick; the hole reaches 12.3 km.

slides.label: the deepest vertical hole ever drilled, reached in 1989
slides.text: Just 23 centimetres wide. The original target was 15,000 metres.
